cells.remarks: Records that the farmers, merchants, etc., of the villages Vijay-nagara-pēṭṭa, jointly, purchased the present village of Kōḍihalli and land in the village of Garbhāyipita in Ponnuṅgaṇḍa-30 to the properties in their villages for various payment of rakshā-śulka to the Muddeya-daṇḍanāyaka, the mahāpradhāna of the king, on whom they conferred the prithvi-kēṭṭana. cells.date: Śaka 969, Sarvajit, Pushya su. 5, Thursday=1047 A.D., December 24.
cells.remarks: Gives a detailed genealogy of the king. Issued from his victorious camp near Kalyāṇa, the most important of the villages inside the camp, namely, Kōṇḍi, situated in the Kōṇḍi-300, granted the land in the village of Garbhāyipita in Ponnuṅgaṇḍa-30 to the gr̥hamaṇḍalī Muṭṭijināya, on the occasion of Makara-Saṅkrānti for renovation, worship and offerings in the Traipurusha temple in Vēhura in Ponnuṅgaṇḍa-30 situated in the Viḷvōla-vishaya and for feeding 200 students and various śivās in the same temple. The charter was written by Jayakāra, the son of Prajñīkara.

cells.remarks: Records the grant of thirty-four artasas of land along with four ploughs from the ordinary land attached to the village of Kiri-kākā in the western district (paśchimamahālakshya) of Ujjain to the Brāhmaṇa Nāyaka Vachchhasama, the son of Brahmasvāmin, of Trivithi who belonged to the Kāṇva-śākhā and had the three gotras, Ātrēya, Archchanānasa and Syāvāśva, who was rich with Vedic studies, who belonged to Baivrichha-śākhā and who was an emigrant from Manyakhēta, by the king from his camp at Dhārā for his own merit as well as for the merit of his parents. Published in the I.H.Q., Vol. VII pp. 305 and plates.

cells.date:
(1) Vikrama 1148, Pausha ba. 15, Sūrya-grahana.

(2) Vikrama 1177, Chaitra śu. --, Friday, Samvat 1120 A.D., March 11.
The tithi ended on the previous day.
cells.remarks: Records the grant of villages Mahatabā and Āmbhasthā to the Brāhmaṇa Nāyaka Mādhavadēvasarman, son of Tripathi Vāyavadeva, of Trivithi. Belonged to the Vātsya-gotra, the three pravaras, Ārushi-śikhiņa, Vāsiśhtha and Maitrā-varuṇa Kauṇḍinya-gotra, Āruṇa-śikhin, Lādanāva and who was an emigrant from Parichhata-mahāsthāna by Mahāmaṇḍalēśhvara Raṇadhavaladēva ruling Purpīṇa-pathaka-1040 on the occasion of the solar eclipse, after taking a bath in the confluence of the rivers Kshiprā and Kālingā at Amarēśvara-kshetra on the first date. The grant was written by the second date by Jayē-bhāṇḍāgāra, probably on orders of Mahākshapatalā Kuntārya. Mentions Di(Purohita) Vāmanasvāmi and Rājaputra Kumārapāla.

cells.remarks: Records the grant of six villages divided into six shares to three brāhmaṇas (names and other details such as śākhā, gōtra, pravara, etc. given) by Pratāpa Gaṅgadēva, after bathing at the confluence of the rivers Rēvā and Kavilā and worshipping Ama-rēśvaradēva, on the order of the king. Published in Ep. Ind., Vol. IX, pp. 117 ff. and plates. Bhāṇḍār-kar's List, No. 559.

cells.remarks: Records the grant of the village Vahadhōvi situated in Payiḍhu-kā-paṭṭala by Rāṇaka Amṛitapāla on the orders of the king after the latter had returned from the river Yamunā at Āsaṭikā. Bhāṭṭāraka Nīlakaṇṭha, the son of Bhaṭṭāraka Kēśavarāśi and the grandson of Paramabhaṭṭāraka Kīrttivāsa, who was a Parama-Pāśupata, and who was a resident of the maṭha of the temple of the god Mahāliṅga at Āsaṭi for the king's own merit as well as that of his parents. The text of the charter was composed by the kāyastha Paṅgita Jagadhara, son of Paṅgita Śrīdhara and the engraver was the goldsmith Ṭhakkura Chuḍāhastika, son of Sādhu Jayapāla.

cells.location: MAHARASHTRA NAGPUR DISTRICT NAGPUR TAHSIL Nāgpur — Maharashtra
cells.place: Stone slab in the Central Archaeological Museum. Findspot: Not known.
cells.remarks: Slightly worn out. Contains a detailed genealogy of the Paramāras of Mālwā from Vairisimha (II). Records that king Naravarmmadēva gave the village of Mōkhalapāṭaka in the two villages in Vijayamandal formerly granted by his brother Lakshmadēva on the occasion of a solar eclipse. Also states that the king ordered Lakshmīdhara to construct a temple (dēvālaya) adorned with eulogies and hymns composed by himself (i.e., the king). Contains an exhortation and the judge poetry. The prasasti was originally engraved and appreciated the same. Published in Ep. Ind., Vol. II, pp. 180 ff.; Bhandarkar's List, No. 170.

cells.location: PUDUKKOTTAI DISTRICT KULATTUR TALUK Nārttāmalai — Tamil Nadu
cells.place: Jambunāthasvāmi temple, mahāmaṇḍapa, south wall, outside.
cells.remarks: Records an undertaking made by the nagarattār of the territorial division of the town to the effect that the people of the nāḍu should pay the tax according to the assessment of their nāḍu was made after their nāḍu was surveyed. It is also laid down that the defaulters should undergo capital punishment and their property should be confiscated and given to the temple of the god Jambunāthar (of the locality). The record is said to have been engraved on these temples of Agnisaram. In characters of about 16th-17th century. Published in the Inscriptions (Texts) of the Pudukkōṭṭai State, No. 922.

cells.remarks: Records the creation of a tax-free endowment (tiruvidaiyāṭṭam) out of the village Kuḍivāyil by the mahāsabhā of the village. The village was included in the Tañjāvūr-tani-kkuṟram-kūṟṟa-vaḷanāḍu included in the Tañjāvūr-tani-kkuṟram-kūṟṟa-vaḷanāḍu in the temple called Tirumēṟkōyil of their own place. The endowed village was entrusted as dēvadānam to Dēvan Periyāṉ alias Mūvēndavēḷāṉ, who is said to have made the temple fit for cultivation. It is stipulated that he should pay annually 75 kaḻam of paddy to the temple for the daily offerings to the god. Also adds the creation (obviously by the same nagarattār) of a flower garden named Uṣḷācchaṉai for the said god.

cells.remarks: Damaged. Records the king's order issued to the nāṭṭār of Teṉkavi [ṟa]-nāḍu informing them of the exemption of taxes granted on certain lands to be effected from the 2[0]th year of the king Sundara-Pāṇḍya to meet the expenses of the [daily] food offerings etc. to Peruṅkāñji [l] lēñchōḻap-Perumāḷi Āḻvār of Saḍaiyāṟ-paṟai. cells.language: Sanskrit and Tamil, Grantha and Vaṭṭeḻuttu
cells.remarks: Fragmentary and worn out. The Sanskrit portion, in the beginning, mentions the appointment of the members of different guilds such as paṭṭinam of eighteen-nāḍu, the thirty-two Vēḷārpuram, etc. Refers, at the end, to a number of persons designated as kavarai iñjīṅgam hailing from different places, such as Tāraṅgāḍi, Māṇabarāntśvaram, etc. In characters of about the 10th century.

Kamudi.—Vaḷivīṭṭaiyāṉar temple, on the side of the Kamudi-Aruppukōṭṭai road, one mile to the west of Kamudi. Right side of the elephant-stone, set up in front of the temple.
text.language: Sanskrit and Tamil, Grantha and Vaṭṭeḻuttu
text.remarks: Fragmentary and worn out. The Sanskrit portion, in the beginning, mentions the appointment of the members of different guilds such as paṭṭinam of eighteen-nāḍu, the thirty-two Vēḷārpuram, etc. Refers, at the end, to a number of persons designated as kavarai iñjīṅgam hailing from different places, such as Tāraṅgāḍi, Māṇabarāntśvaram, etc. In characters of about the 10th century.Read more (1 KB)

cells.king: Śaḍaiyavarman Sundara Pāṇḍya (I) who was pleased to seize all the counties.
cells.date: Regnal year 13, Mina 7, śu. 7, Mṛgaśīrsha, Monday, 27 February 1262 A.D. It was Mina 5.
cells.remarks: Records that the authorities of the temple of the deity Deyvachchi-laipparuḷāl at Tiruppullāṇi in Śembāṇāḍu received Veṇḍiyūr-uḍaiyāṉ-Kōmāṉ-Aḻagiya-Maṇavāḷa-dāsar alias Tūṇḍāṉiṅgār of Kaḷattūr alias Nakkiṉallūr in Śevirukā-nāḍu and undertook to meet the expenses of various food offerings to the said deity and consort Puruṇḍirunīr being set up in the temple during the (1) daily service of the sandhi-sandhi (2) monthly bathing of the deities on the days of Uttirāṣṭādi, the donor's natal star; and (3) the festival of the days of Arpaśi, in the month of the donor's birth.

cells.location: Pāgamalai
cells.place: Tālāgīśvara temple, base stones around the central shrine.
cells.remarks: In verse. Traces the origin of the dynasty from the Creator of the Universe; records the eulogy of the ruling king; endows him with the title Mahēśvaracūḍāmaṇi and prays for the God Māhēśvara's perpetual presence in the temple, in question, named as Mahēśvaracūḍāmaṇi-Pallavēśvara. The middle portion of the record has been published in Ep. Ind., Vol. XIX, pp. 113 ff.

NANNILAM TALUK

Śēṅgāḷipuram.—Duṇḍubhīśvara temple, central shrine, north and west walls, tiers.
cells.remarks: Highly damaged and peeled off. Seems to record an undertaking of a gift of land for the maintenance of the temple, lamps, etc., of the temple of the god Duṇḍuṇīśvara-uḍaiyār to be kept as a perpetual lamp in the temple, by receiving 2700 kāśu from a person (name lost) who probably caused the temple to be constructed. Cf. A.R.Ep., 1973-74, No. B 221. In characters of about the 12th-13th century.

cells.place: West wall of the same shrine, base tier.
cells.remarks: Stones disturbed and missing and partly built in. Commences with the king's sanskrit praśasti beginning Samasta-jagat-ēkavīra, etc. Contains the eulogy of the king, registering the sale of 1000 avvāḍu karukku by the nattavār of a village in Seṛṛūr-kūrram in Kuḷakāḷapuram, a dattam parisatta nagaram in Seṛṛūr-kūrram included in Kuḷōttuṅga-vaḷanāḍu in favour of the temples of the deities (1) Paramāṇḍīśvaram-uḍaiyār at Paḷḷichchan-daṇḍa-grāmam and (2) Adipūrīśvaram-uḍaiyār-uḍaiyār-only 27 kuḷi for the latter in the form of a house site. Cf. ibid-No. B 223.

cells.location: AHMADABAD DISTRICT AHMADABAD CITY TALUKA Ahmadābād
cells.place: Tomb of Malik Sh‘abān, Rakhyāl. Slab on the left side of the western gate.
cells.remarks: Contains the text of a farmān stating that at the request of the loyal and favourite servant of the king, Malik Sh‘abān, entitled Malik’sh-Sharq Malik ‘Imādu’l-Mulk, the Pay-Master of the empire (‘Ārid-i-Mamālik son of Malik Tughā Sultāni entitled Tāj’ul-Mulk, six ploughs (jūf/iwar) land in the village (mauḍa) of Rakhyāl (in the Haveli of Ahmadābād) (Ahmadābād district) of the magnificent city of Ahmadābād in which the Malik had dug wells, planted trees, made channels and built pavilions for the recreation of the elite, was ordered by the king to be granted in perpetuity to the Malik and his descendants. It further enjoins upon the officials (Ummal) of the said, district to leave it along with the garden, wells and trees to the descendants, both on son’s and daughter’s side, of the Malik and not cause any inconvenience to them. Published, Ep. Ind. Mos., 1921-22, p. 3, without plate.

cells.place: contd. BARODA DISTRICT—concld. BARODA TALUKA—concld. Khajuri.—Masjid in the Bazar. Slab in the north wall. (Impression received from the Superintending Archaeologist, Western Circle, Baroda).
cells.remarks: Contains the text of a Will made by Sayyid Ḥidāyatullāh son of Sayyid Ḥasan, who states that he had constructed a mosque and Bārā Miyān, that he owned a Kanba rent-free land situated outside the royal fort and adjacent to the Laḥrīpura Gate outside the city near the Chandan-Tank, that it was the inherited property and he bequeathed it to the mosque and full sense, granted it out of his own free-will and in full sense, bequeathed that land except the mosque, which was a waqf as well as five Kanba land at Ḥamīdpur, nine-ten shops four houses and one grave of Jachā Mā jī built by him for his son who had descended from him to hold in perpetuity with a right to gift it away to anybody or make an outright sale, (the only condition being that) the maintenance of the mosque would be their responsibility. Date that writing.

cells.place: Slab in the wall of a room attached to the Dargāh of Hadrat Muṣṭafā-kūshī Naqshband, in Mahalla Khānyār.
cells.remarks: Modern. Records the names of the following ladies of the (Naqshbandī) family buried in the tomb of Hadrat-i-Naqshband: (1) Gul Begam, daughter of Jahāngīr Bādshāh (Ghāzī and wife of Hadrat Khwāja Mu‘īn-ud-Dīn Hādī Naqshbandī (2) Begam Ṣāhiba (i.e., wife) of Hadrat Khwāja Sharaf-ud-Dīn Ṣāhib, of the Chaghatā’iya family. (3) Begam Ṣāhiba of Khwāja Niẓām-ud-Dīn Jānī, daughter of Khwāja Raḥmat-ullāh Khān, the Pay-Master General (Mīr Bakhshī) of Hindustān in the reign of ‘Ālamgīr Bādshāh Ghāzī (i.e., Aurangzeb). (4) Begam Ṣāhiba of Khwāja Niẓām-ud-Dīn Muḥammad, daughter of Hadrat ‘Ālamgīr Bādshāh Ghāzī. (5) Begam Ṣāhiba of Janāb Khwāja Nūr-ud-Dīn Muḥammad Āfāb Naqshbandī, daughter of Mīrzā Aḥmad ‘Alī Chaghatā’ī. The information is stated to have been copied from the Tuḥfa-i-Naqshbandīya.

cells.remarks: Damaged. Records the construction of a Khānqā, a mosque and a tank in the path of Allāh and His Prophet, by Sayyid Ḥasan, the Quṭb (lit. Pole-star) and spiritual guide of the people of Dakhan (i.e. Deccan). The saint also constructed a water-reservoir (chashma) to the memory of Imām Ḥasan (grandson of the Prophet) on the green day (i.e. ‘Urs) of Imām Ḥasan. ‘Alī Ḥasan Ḥājjī, the grandson of the saint, was guided by Raḥmān Qulī Baig. Cf. Memoirs Arch. Sur. Ind., No. 49, pp. 77-78, No. 3299 (a), pl. VIII.

cells.location: UTTAR PRADESH DEHRADUN DISTRICT DEHRADUN TAHSIL Dehrādūn — Uttar Pradesh
cells.place: Gurudwārā Rām Rāi. Slab in the wall of one of the Dālāns.
cells.date: Regnal year 31 (words), A.H. 1099 (words and chronogram), Bhādrapada su. 6, Sunday = 1688 A.D., August 23
cells.remarks: Gives an account of the circumstances which led to the succession of Gurū Rām Rāi after Gurū Har-Rāi, the eighth Gurū, the foundation of the said Gurudwārā and the various buildings therein. States that Dārā Shukūh subsequently gave his defeat at the hands of Aurangzeb in the war of succession, going to Gurū Har-Rāi, the eighth line of the great gnostic and a disciple of the Gurū, ultimately fled towards Multān. The Gurū, summoned by the emperor to the royal court, excused himself due to infirmity but, in compliance with the royal wishes, that he should send the best one from among his sons and followers, sent Gurū Rām Rāi. The emperor had a meeting with the boy, sent Gurū Rām Rāi. The emperor had a meeting with the boy, and was greatly pleased with his answers to his questions, showed great favours to him. After some time Rām Rāi sought and obtained the emperor's permission to leave and returned to his Master after receiving robes of honour. After the death of the Master, Rām Rāi went to Āgra where the emperor, again, gave him land on the bank of the tank (Ṭālāb) of Āgra, and he him lodgings on the bank of the tank (Ṭālāb) of Āgra. Here he stayed for twenty years. At the thought of impending death, he selected the village Kaḥrada in a fertile and pleasant valley in the mountains of Garhwāl, God-rāj-rhiwāl as his last resting place. Faith singeth, the ruler of the place, granted this and four other villages to him. Two months before his death, the Gurū took another wife, Panjābū by name. The text at this stage refers to the setting up of a wooden pillar (mīnār). When Gurū died on the given date, his disciple ( ? ) cremated once the place of his death, another at the place of bathing (his dead body ?) and also at his samādh (place of cremation or burial). A garden was also laid out. Also states that the site has become a place of pilgrimage for all and sundry. Name of the composer of the text unintelligible.
